blogs.title: The Persistence of Interest: Standing and Mootness in Government Penalty Claims
blogs.description: This post analyzes the Eighth Circuit's nuanced approach to Article III standing and mootness regarding statutory penalties. When a plaintiff is made whole through the payment of back wages and liquidated damages, does their 'personal interest' in a government-collected penalty survive? The blog explores the tension between the deterrent function of civil penalties (as seen in Friends of the Earth v. Laidlaw) and the requirement for a continuing personal stake in litigation.

blogs.title: The 'Legislature Knows How' Test: Limits of Private Enforcement in State Wage Acts
blogs.description: Focusing on the court's ruling regarding the Minnesota Payment of Wages Act (MPWA), this post discusses the judicial application of statutory construction. It examines how courts determine whether an aggrieved party has a private right to seek penalties when the statute only grants that power to a state commissioner. The post will delve into the significance of the 'legislature knows how' doctrine as a tool for interpreting the scope of private rights of action.

blogs.title: Procedural Boundaries: Why New Remedies Cannot Be 'Briefed-In'
blogs.description: This post examines the procedural implications of the court's refusal to grant injunctive relief because the request was not included in the original complaint. It explores the distinction between the scope of a complaint and the arguments presented in summary judgment briefs, highlighting the importance of Rule 15 and the court's role in maintaining the boundaries of the issues properly submitted for adjudication.
